name: Peter Harisiades
bio: Peter Harisiades was a Greek-born, long-resident American Communist and labor journalist ordered deported under the McCarran Internal Security Act for his past Party membership, facing what supporters warned was near-certain death if returned to Greece. His became the lead test case, Harisiades v. Shaughnessy (1952), in which the Supreme Court upheld the deportation of long-time residents for former Communist affiliation.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran (Internal Security) Act for past Communist Party membership.
convicted: Ordered deported; the Supreme Court upheld the order in Harisiades v. Shaughnessy (1952).
sentence: Deportation; held and fought for years.

name: David Hyun
bio: David Hyun was a Korean-American architect held without bail on Terminal Island from the McCarran Act midnight raids of October 1950, one of four Los Angeles detainees fought over in a long bail battle that reached the Supreme Court. He faced deportation for his radical and labor associations.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran Act for alleged Communist affiliation.
convicted: Held without bail from October 1950; deportation proceedings.
sentence: Detention pending deportation; ultimately not deported.

name: Harry Carlisle
bio: Harry Carlisle was an English-born novelist, journalist, and lecturer held without bail on Terminal Island under the McCarran Act, one of the Los Angeles deportation detainees seized in the October 1950 raids and fighting removal for his radical politics.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran Act for alleged Communist affiliation.
convicted: Held without bail from October 1950; deportation hearings began May 1951.

name: Frank Carlson
bio: Frank Carlson was a trade unionist held without bail on Terminal Island under the McCarran Act, one of the Los Angeles foreign-born detainees facing deportation for political and labor activity after the October 1950 raids.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran Act for alleged Communist affiliation.
convicted: Held without bail from October 1950; deportation proceedings.

name: Miriam Stevenson
bio: Miriam Stevenson was a former union organizer held without bail on Terminal Island under the McCarran Act — one of the Los Angeles deportation detainees of the October 1950 raids — whose son was inducted into the Army while she sat jailed facing deportation for her politics.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran Act for alleged Communist affiliation.
convicted: Held without bail from October 1950; deportation proceedings.

name: Ernesto Mangaoang
bio: Ernesto Mangaoang was a business agent and leader of ILWU Local 37, the Seattle-based Filipino cannery workers' union. Arrested by federal immigration authorities in the late 1940s and held under the McCarran Act, he faced years of legal battles over the government's effort to deport him as an alien. His fight produced the landmark case Mangaoang v. Boyd and the 1954 U.S. Supreme Court decision International Longshoremen's & Warehousemen's Union v. Boyd, which held that Filipinos who had come to the United States as U.S. nationals before Philippine independence could not be deported as aliens — clarifying the immigration status of some 70,000 Filipino Americans.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran Act as an alleged Communist and militant union leader (ILWU Local 37); arrested by immigration authorities in the late 1940s and held in the King County Jail.
convicted: No criminal conviction; deportation defeated in Mangaoang v. Boyd / ILWU v. Boyd (1954).

name: Knut Heikkinen
bio: Knut Heikkinen was a Finnish-American radical held in the St. Louis County jail in Duluth under the McCarran Act, facing deportation for his Communist and labor associations.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran Act for alleged Communist affiliation.
convicted: Held without bail; long deportation fight.

name: John Zydok
bio: John Zydok, a Detroit Communist born in the old Russian empire, was the subject of one of the first deportation orders issued under the new McCarran Act and was held in the Wayne County jail; a federal appeals court ordered him freed on bail.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran Act for Communist Party membership.
convicted: Among the first McCarran Act deportation orders (1950); appealed.
sentence: Detention pending deportation; ordered released on bail.

name: George Siskind
bio: George Siskind, a Polish-born writer and teacher, was among the first people ordered deported under the McCarran Act in December 1950 for alleged Communist Party membership.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran Act for alleged Communist Party membership.
convicted: Among the first McCarran Act deportation orders (Dec. 1950); appealed.

name: Rose Nelson Lightcap
bio: Rose Nelson Lightcap, an official of the Jewish People's Fraternal Order, was among the first people ordered deported under the McCarran Act in December 1950 for her radical affiliations.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran Act for alleged Communist/radical affiliation.
convicted: Among the first McCarran Act deportation orders (Dec. 1950); appealed.

name: Manuel Tarazona
bio: Manuel Tarazona was one of the 39 foreign-born radicals re-arrested when the Civil Rights Congress bail fund was revoked in 1951; held for deportation after bail was twice refused, he was ordered released on bond by Judge Edward Weinfeld, who called the refusals an abuse of discretion.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran Act for alleged Communist affiliation.
convicted: Held for deportation; ordered released on bail.

name: Sol Hertz
bio: Sol Hertz was a New York Farmers Union leader placed under threat of deportation under the McCarran Act for his political associations.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran Act for alleged Communist/radical affiliation.
convicted: Faced deportation proceedings (1951).

name: Maurice Travis
bio: Maurice Travis was the secretary-treasurer of the left-led International Union of Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers, who had earlier lost an eye in an anti-Communist attack. In the 1951 Empire Zinc strike in Grant County, New Mexico — later dramatized in the film Salt of the Earth — he was convicted of criminal contempt for defying an anti-picketing injunction.
charges: Criminal contempt of court — defying an anti-picketing injunction during the Empire Zinc strike.
convicted: Convicted of contempt (1951).

name: Clinton Jencks
bio: Clinton Jencks was the Mine-Mill international representative who led the Empire Zinc strike of Mexican-American miners in Grant County, New Mexico — the strike depicted in Salt of the Earth. Convicted of contempt during the strike, he was later prosecuted for allegedly false Taft-Hartley non-Communist affidavits in the case that became the landmark Jencks v. United States (1957).
charges: Criminal contempt of court during the Empire Zinc strike (and, later, a Taft-Hartley affidavit prosecution).
convicted: Convicted of contempt (1951); later won Jencks v. United States (1957).

name: James Lustig
bio: James Lustig was a United Electrical Workers organizer awaiting trial in 1951 for inciting to riot during the 1946 Phelps-Dodge copper strike in Elizabeth, New Jersey. He had already served a contempt jail term as an official of the Joint Anti-Fascist Refugee Committee who refused to name the committee's donors.
charges: Inciting to riot (1946 Phelps-Dodge strike); earlier, contempt for refusing to name anti-fascist committee donors.
convicted: Previously jailed for contempt; awaiting trial for inciting to riot (1951).
sentence: A prior contempt jail term; faced strike-related charges.

name: Theodore Narusheff
bio: Theodore Narusheff was a union organizer convicted of atrocious assault in February 1951 — five years after the 1946 Phelps-Dodge copper strike in Elizabeth, New Jersey, in which company gunmen shot strikers but only strikers were prosecuted.
charges: Atrocious assault arising from the 1946 Phelps-Dodge strike.
convicted: Convicted in February 1951, five years after the alleged offense.
sentence: Imprisonment for the strike-related assault charge.

name: Philip Bart
bio: Philip Bart was the general manager of the Communist Daily Worker, convicted of contempt of Congress in 1951 (on 8 of 32 counts) for refusing to answer the House Un-American Activities Committee's questions.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC (Daily Worker general manager).
convicted: Convicted on 8 of 32 contempt counts (1951).
sentence: A jail term for contempt of Congress.

name: Irving Feiner
bio: Irving Feiner was a Syracuse University student arrested for a sidewalk speech publicizing a Young Progressives meeting and criticizing local officials. His disorderly-conduct conviction was upheld 6-3 by the Supreme Court in the landmark free-speech case Feiner v. New York (1951); he served thirty days and was expelled from the university.
charges: Disorderly conduct (incitement) — for a political street-corner speech.
convicted: Yes — conviction upheld by the Supreme Court in Feiner v. New York (1951).

name: Charles Nusser
bio: Charles Nusser was the New Jersey Communist Party secretary arrested in early 1951 under a 1918 state anti-subversive statute for handing out leaflets urging negotiation to end the Korean War. His bail was set at $30,000, then reduced to $1,500, and he was re-arrested in the campaign against the leafleting.
charges: Violating a 1918 New Jersey anti-subversive statute — for distributing Korean War peace leaflets.
convicted: Arrested and prosecuted; charges contested.
sentence: Held on bail; faced up to two years.

name: Olava Skottedal
bio: Olava Skottedal was arrested in Babylon, Long Island in 1951 for distributing the National Guardian and an American Labor Party peace petition; held on $500 bail and denied a jury trial, she faced up to two years and a $1,000 fine for the leafleting.
charges: Distributing literature / a peace petition — under a local ordinance.
convicted: Arrested and prosecuted; denied a jury trial.
sentence: Held on $500 bail; faced up to two years.

name: Martin Robbins
bio: Martin Robbins, a World War II veteran, was arrested with Olava Skottedal in Babylon, Long Island in 1951 for distributing the National Guardian and an American Labor Party peace petition, and faced up to two years for the leafleting.
charges: Distributing literature / a peace petition — under a local ordinance.
convicted: Arrested and prosecuted; denied a jury trial.
sentence: Held on $500 bail; faced up to two years.

name: Marcel Scherer
affiliation: New York Labor Conference for Peace
bio: Marcel Scherer, coordinator of the New York Labor Conference for Peace, was tried for contempt of Congress after refusing to answer 52 questions from the House Un-American Activities Committee. He was acquitted in 1951 when the judge ruled he had been within his rights.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC's questions.
convicted: No — acquitted in 1951.

name: Louise Berman
bio: Louise Berman was an American Labor Party leader prosecuted for contempt of Congress for refusing to answer the House Un-American Activities Committee; she was acquitted in 1951.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC.
convicted: No — acquitted in 1951.

name: Eugene Brunner
bio: Eugene M. Brunner was prosecuted for contempt for refusing to say whether he had belonged to the Communist Party in 1937–39; his six-month sentence was upheld in 1951.
charges: Contempt — for refusing to answer questions about Communist Party membership.
convicted: Convicted; six-month sentence upheld (1951).

name: Roosevelt Ward
bio: Roosevelt Ward Jr. was a young Black leader of the Labor Youth League prosecuted in New Orleans for failing to notify his draft board of a change of address — a charge his supporters saw as a political reprisal. He drew a three-year sentence and was freed on $15,000 bail pending appeal.
charges: Selective Service violation — failing to notify his draft board of a change of address.
convicted: Convicted; sentenced to three years (on appeal).
sentence: Three years; released on $15,000 bail pending appeal.

name: Robert Michener
bio: Robert Michener was a nineteen-year-old Quaker and Drake University student sentenced to ten years in federal prison in 1951 for refusing to be drafted on religious grounds.
charges: Refusing induction into the armed forces (conscientious objection on religious grounds).
convicted: Convicted in federal court, Topeka, Kansas.

name: Edward Honeycutt
bio: Edward Honeycutt was a Black man sentenced to death for rape in Opelousas, Louisiana, whose case the Civil Rights Congress took up as a racial frame-up amid a wave of Louisiana death sentences imposed on Black men for that charge.
charges: Rape — a capital charge his defenders called a racial frame-up.
convicted: Convicted and sentenced to death; appealed with CRC support.

name: Jerry Newson
bio: Jerry Newson was a nineteen-year-old Oakland shoeshine worker sentenced to death for a double murder, in a case the Civil Rights Congress publicized as a frame-up built on a coerced confession and tainted identification. After years of campaigning his conviction was overturned.
charges: Double murder — a capital conviction his defenders called a frame-up.
convicted: Convicted and sentenced to death; conviction later reversed after appeals.

name: Paul Washington
bio: Paul Washington was a Black man sentenced to death for rape in Gretna, Louisiana, one of a series of Louisiana capital cases the Civil Rights Congress challenged as racial frame-ups; the CRC carried his appeal toward the Supreme Court.
charges: Rape — a capital charge his defenders called a racial frame-up.
convicted: Convicted and sentenced to death; appealed with CRC support.

name: Theodore Jordan
bio: Theodore Jordan was a Black man convicted in 1932 of murdering a dining-car steward in Klamath Falls, Oregon, on a confession he said was beaten out of him; sentenced to hang, his sentence was commuted to life in 1934. In 1951 his case was reopened, and an official inquiry found that racial prejudice had prevented a fair prosecution.
charges: Murder — a conviction on an allegedly coerced confession, found tainted by racial prejudice.
convicted: Convicted 1932 (death, commuted to life 1934); case reopened 1951.
sentence: Death, commuted to life; pardon sought.

name: Mack Ingram
bio: Mack Ingram was a Black North Carolina farmer convicted of assault for allegedly leering at a white girl from a distance of seventy-five feet — a case that became a national symbol of Jim Crow absurdity and injustice. He was given a two-year sentence and appealed.
charges: Assault on a female (by 'leering') — a Jim Crow prosecution for looking at a white girl from 75 feet away.
convicted: Convicted; two-year sentence (under appeal).

name: Lawrence Walker
bio: Lawrence Walker was a Black former Air Force sergeant convicted of a double murder near Riverside, California and sentenced to life at San Quentin, in a case the Civil Rights Congress and the National Guardian publicized as a racial frame-up of an innocent man tried in a Jim Crow atmosphere.
charges: Double murder — a conviction his defenders called a racial frame-up.
convicted: Convicted; sentenced to life imprisonment (appeal pending).

name: Camille DeRose
bio: Mrs. Camille DeRose was the owner of a Cicero, Illinois apartment building who rented to a Black family, the Harvey Clarks, triggering the violent July 1951 white riot. In a notorious inversion, a Cook County grand jury indicted DeRose and others for 'conspiracy' to lower property values by renting to a Negro, rather than the white mob.
charges: 'Conspiracy to injure property' — for renting an apartment to a Black family in Cicero, Illinois.
convicted: Indicted 1951 (the indictments were later dropped amid national outrage).
sentence: Faced up to a year; indictment ultimately dismissed.

name: Norman Silverman
bio: Norman Silverman was arrested for distributing leaflets headed 'End Mob Rule in Cicero' after the 1951 anti-Black housing riot, and was then swept into the Cook County grand jury's 'conspiracy' indictment that targeted the Clarks' supporters instead of the white rioters.
charges: 'Conspiracy' — after distributing leaflets condemning the Cicero racial riot.
convicted: Indicted 1951 (indictments later dropped).
sentence: Faced up to a year; indictment ultimately dismissed.

name: Dirk Struik
bio: Dirk Jan Struik was a world-renowned MIT mathematician and historian of science indicted by a Middlesex County grand jury in 1951 under a Massachusetts sedition law for conspiring to overthrow the state and federal governments. He was suspended from MIT; the charges were eventually dropped after the Supreme Court's 1956 Nelson decision voided state sedition laws.
charges: Massachusetts sedition law — conspiring to overthrow the state and federal governments.
convicted: Indicted 1951; charges dropped after Pennsylvania v. Nelson (1956).
sentence: None — charges dismissed; he was suspended from MIT for years.

name: Harry Winner
bio: Harry E. Winner was a Massachusetts businessman indicted alongside the MIT mathematician Dirk Struik in 1951 under the state sedition law for conspiring to overthrow the government; the charges were later dropped.
charges: Massachusetts sedition law — conspiring to overthrow the government (co-defendant of Dirk Struik).
convicted: Indicted 1951; charges later dropped.

name: Leon Gilbert
bio: Lieutenant Leon A. Gilbert was a Black officer of the segregated 24th Infantry Regiment court-martialed in Korea in 1950 for 'misbehavior before the enemy' after refusing what he called a suicidal order. Sentenced to death in a case the NAACP and Civil Rights Congress decried as a racial scapegoating, he had his sentence commuted by President Truman to 20 years.
charges: 'Misbehavior before the enemy' (refusing an order) — court-martial of a Black officer of the segregated 24th Infantry.
convicted: Convicted; sentenced to death, commuted by Truman to 20 years.

name: Pasquale Branca
bio: Pasquale Branca was a former teacher prosecuted for contempt for refusing to answer the House Un-American Activities Committee; in 1951 he was freed on a ruling that he had a constitutional right to refuse to answer.
charges: Contempt — for refusing to answer HUAC's questions.
convicted: No — freed on a ruling upholding his right to refuse.

name: Sidney Buchman
bio: Sidney Buchman was a leading Hollywood screenwriter (Mr. Smith Goes to Washington) who, before the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1951, admitted his own past Communist membership but refused to name anyone else — calling it repugnant to inform. He was later cited and convicted of contempt of Congress for the refusal.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to name others before HUAC.
convicted: Cited for contempt (1951); later convicted.
sentence: A fine and suspended sentence; blacklisted.
